transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I’m here mostly because my family and a few people around me keep saying I’ve been doing too much. But honestly, from where I’m standing, it doesn’t feel like “too much” so much as finally getting things moving the way they ought to be moved.

We’ve got this move to handle, and if I don’t keep after every box, every list, every little detail, it just sits there. And then there’s the new garage — I don’t want it thrown together sloppy, I want it rebuilt right, with a proper setup, the way a man can actually use it. On top of that I’ve been helping organize things at church, because somebody has to keep people on track there too. And even at work, I still try to show the younger fellows how the job ought to be done, because they rush or they miss steps, and I’ve been around long enough to know better.

So I guess that’s why I’m here. Everybody says I’m pushing too hard, taking on too much, but to me it feels like I’m the only one with enough drive to get it all handled.
Do you often feel like you're the only one who really knows how to get things done properly?

Yes, I do, if I’m being honest. I don’t mean that to sound arrogant, but it’s just… when something needs doing, I can see all the pieces of it. Other people seem to look at one box or one errand or one little task and think that’s enough, but I’m looking at the whole thing.

With the move, for example, there are boxes, labels, what goes where, what has to be done first, what can’t be left until the last minute — and if I don’t keep pushing, it just drifts. Same with the garage. I don’t want some half-done setup where tools are piled in a corner and nothing makes sense. I want it rebuilt properly, laid out right, usable.

And church too — people mean well, but somebody has to organize things or everyone just talks in circles. Then at work, I still try to show the younger fellows the right way, because they cut corners or don’t think ahead. So yes, I suppose I do feel like I’m the one with enough drive to actually get things done the way they should be.
Do you feel like your efforts to get everything done are causing you a lot of stress or anxiety?

Stress or anxiety… I don’t know that I’d call it that, exactly. I mean, I get worked up when things aren’t being handled right, sure. Anybody would, if they saw things sliding or people standing around waiting for someone else to make a decision.

But it doesn’t feel to me like worry, like I’m sitting there scared or panicking. It’s more like there’s a lot to do and I can see it all, so I keep moving. Maybe other people look at that and say I’m stressed, but from my side it feels more like pressure to keep everything from turning into a mess.

So… I’m not sure. I haven’t really thought of it as anxiety. More like frustration when folks don’t keep up.
Do you feel like things have to be done exactly your way in order for them to be done correctly?

Well… “exactly my way” sounds a little harsher than I’d put it, but yes, I suppose there’s truth in that. It feels like I can already see how something ought to be done, start to finish, and when people start questioning every step or trying to do it some sideways way, I get… I get pretty impatient.

Lately it’s been more than just wanting things orderly. I’ll be in a great mood, joking around, feeling like I’ve got all the energy in the world, like I’m ten feet tall and can carry the whole thing myself. And then somebody — my wife, or my boy — asks one little question, something simple like why I’m doing it that way or whether it can wait, and I snap. I don’t always mean to, but it comes out like, “Either get on board with what I’m doing or get out of my way.”

Because in that moment it doesn’t feel like they’re helping. It feels like they’re slowing me down. And I know that probably sounds difficult to live with, but when I’m in it, I just feel so sure that my plan is the right one and everybody else needs to catch up.
Are your relationships with family or friends being affected by your behavior or the way you're handling things lately?

Yes… it has. I don’t like admitting that, because in my head I’m just trying to keep things moving and make sure nobody drops the ball, but yes, it’s affected things.

At work, it got bad enough that they pulled me off after a safety incident. I was sure I had things under control, and I didn’t see it the way they saw it at the time, but afterward everybody acted like I couldn’t be trusted to make the right call. That was humiliating. I’ve worked hard my whole life, and then suddenly people are looking at me like I’m a problem.

And at home… my wife and family have definitely changed how they deal with me. They don’t really trust me with certain decisions right now — money, driving, even parts of the move. They’ll say they’re just being careful, or that things have gotten out of hand, but it feels like they’re taking over. If I want to make a purchase or decide when we’re going somewhere or how the move should be handled, there’s this pause, this look between them, like they’ve already decided I’m not being reasonable.

So yes, my relationships are strained. My wife is tired, my family is wary around me, and I can feel that. I still think a lot of what I was trying to do needed doing, but I can’t really say it hasn’t caused trouble, because it has.
Do you find yourself repeating certain thoughts or behaviors over and over, even when you try to stop?

Repeating thoughts or behaviors… I’m not sure I know exactly what you mean by that.

I don’t think I have, like, a ritual or something I’m doing over and over because I can’t stop myself. I’m not counting things or checking a lock twenty times, if that’s what you’re asking. At least, not that I’ve noticed.

Now, I do get stuck on things in the sense that if something needs doing, I’ll keep coming back to it in my head, and I’ll talk about it more than other people probably want me to. My wife might say I repeat myself, because I’ll keep explaining why something has to be handled a certain way. But from my side, that feels more like trying to get the point across, not like some thought I’m trying to stop and can’t.

So… no, I don’t think so. Not in the way you’re describing, unless I’m misunderstanding the question.
Do you think your way of handling things is causing you more problems than it's solving?

Yes… I think I have to admit that it is. I don’t like saying that, because when I’m doing it, it feels like I’m solving the problem. It feels like I’m the one moving things along while everybody else is standing around talking it to death. But then afterward there’s a bill, or an argument, or somebody upset with me, and I can see it’s made more mess than it fixed.

Like with the garage work and some equipment — I went ahead and put deposits down without really sitting down with my wife and talking it through. In my mind, I was thinking, “If I don’t move on this now, we’ll miss the chance, or the work won’t get done, or it’ll cost more later.” It felt practical to me at the time, even responsible in a way. But I didn’t stop and think how it would feel to her, finding out money had already been committed and she hadn’t been part of the decision. So instead of getting something handled, I created a whole other problem at home.

And the same thing happened with the driving back and forth between the houses. People were telling me I was doing too much, that I was taking chances, and I heard them, but I didn’t really take it in. I kept thinking, “It has to get done, and I’m the one who can do it.” Same at the plant — I was rushing jobs, pushing through, even after people warned me I was cutting it too close or taking risks. I thought I was being efficient. Looking back, I can see how it looked reckless.

So yes, if I’m being honest, my way of handling things has caused more problems than I meant it to. I still have this feeling like things won’t get done right unless I stay on top of them, but I can’t deny that I’ve caused trouble by charging ahead.
Do you find that your attention to details and desire for things to be done a certain way interferes with your ability to complete tasks efficiently?

I don’t know that I’d put it that way exactly.

I mean, I do like things done correctly. I’ve worked around machinery and jobs where if somebody skips a step or does it sloppy, it can matter. So I’ve always paid attention to how things are done, and I can get irritated if people act like “close enough” is good enough. But I don’t think I’m sitting there polishing one tiny detail so long that nothing gets finished.

If anything, lately people would probably say I’m going too fast, not too slow. My problem hasn’t felt like getting stuck on details — it’s more that I see what needs doing and I want it handled, and I don’t have much patience for waiting around or rehashing it over and over.

Now, maybe my wife would say I have a certain way I want things done and I push that too hard. I can see that. If I think a job should be done in a particular order, I’ll keep explaining it, and I may not leave much room for somebody else’s way. But in my mind that’s about being efficient, not being unable to finish.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed that attention to details is keeping me from completing tasks efficiently. If there’s interference, it’s probably more in how I deal with people when I think something needs to get done a certain way.
Do you feel like your behavior or the way you've been handling things lately is significantly impacting your daily life or relationships in a negative way?

Yes. I mean… yes, it has. I wish I could say it was just people overreacting or not understanding what I was trying to do, but it’s gotten to the point where there have been real consequences.

At work, I ended up being pulled off after a safety incident. That’s not a small thing. I’ve worked around equipment for years, so being told I couldn’t keep going because of how I was handling things — that hit me hard. In my head I thought I was just moving fast and getting things done, but other people saw it as unsafe, and apparently it was serious enough that they took me out of it.

And at home it’s affected just about everything. My wife and family don’t really trust me right now with decisions — money decisions, driving back and forth, things about the move. They’ve started stepping in or questioning me because they feel like things got out of hand. I don’t like being treated like I can’t make my own choices, but I also can’t pretend they’re making it up. I did make decisions without talking them through, and I pushed ahead when people were telling me to slow down.

So yes, it’s impacted my daily life and relationships. It’s caused arguments, it’s made my family nervous around my judgment, and it’s affected my work. That’s hard for me to admit, but it’s true.
Do you feel like things would fall apart or not meet your standards if you weren't in charge of them?

Yes… I suppose I do feel that way. Maybe more than I want to admit.

It’s not like I wake up thinking, “I have to control everything.” I don’t see it that way in the moment. What I feel is that there are all these things that need doing, and if I don’t push them forward, they’re either not going to happen, or they’re going to be done halfway. The move, for example — there’s just so much involved, and I keep thinking, “Somebody has to keep this moving.” And with the new garage, I want it rebuilt right, not patched together or delayed until everyone forgets what needed to be done.

And it’s not only at home. At church, if things are disorganized, I start seeing what needs to be arranged and who should be doing what, and I feel like I can help get it straightened out. Then at work, with the younger fellows, I find myself wanting to show them how the job ought to be done, because I’ve been doing this kind of work a long time and I know when someone is cutting corners or not thinking ahead.

So yes, I’m here because everyone says I’ve been doing too much, but from inside my own head it feels more like I’m the only one with enough drive to keep all these things from slipping. I know that probably sounds arrogant, and I don’t mean it that way. It just feels like if I step back, things won’t be handled the way they should be.
Do you feel like things have to be perfect, or as close to perfect as possible, for you to consider them done?

Perfect? No… I don’t think I’d use that word.

I mean, there are things I want done properly. If something is supposed to be level, safe, lined up, measured right — then yes, I don’t like calling it finished if it’s obviously wrong. That’s just how I was brought up and how I worked. In the kind of work I’ve done, you can’t just say, “Well, it’s mostly okay,” if mostly okay means somebody gets hurt or the machine doesn’t run right.

But “perfect” sounds like I’m standing there unable to move on because one little thing is off, and I don’t really see myself that way. I’m not saying every screw has to shine or every corner has to look brand new before I’ll accept it. I can live with things being good enough if they’re actually good enough.

What bothers me is when people say something is done and I can tell they rushed it or skipped parts, or they didn’t think through what happens next. Then I have a hard time letting it go. I’ll keep pointing it out, and maybe I push too much, because in my mind I’m thinking, “If we’re doing it, why not do it right the first time?”

So… no, not perfect exactly. But I do have a pretty firm idea of what “done right” means, and I don’t always trust other people’s version of “done.”
Do you often feel like you're superior to others or have a stronger sense of self-importance than those around you?

I don’t know that I’d say “superior.” That word makes me uncomfortable, honestly. I don’t walk around thinking I’m better than everybody else as a person, or that I’m more important in some grand way.

But… I can see how I might come across like that. Especially when I’m convinced I know the right way something should be handled. I’ve got a lot of years behind me, I’ve done hard work, I’ve had to learn by doing, and sometimes when someone younger or less experienced is making a decision, I catch myself thinking, “No, no, that’s not right — you’re missing the obvious thing here.” And I probably don’t always say that gently.

So if you mean, do I sometimes believe my judgment is better than other people’s in certain situations? Yes, probably. I do. I don’t think that’s the same as feeling superior overall, but maybe the people around me don’t feel the difference when I’m pushing my opinion. They just hear me acting like I know best.

I guess I’d put it this way: I don’t feel like I’m above people, but I do have trouble stepping back when I think I understand something better than they do. And maybe that can look like self-importance from the outside.
Do you feel anxious or uncomfortable when things are not done exactly as you envisioned them?

I’m not sure I’d call it anxious exactly. Uncomfortable, yes, sometimes. It depends what it is.

If I’ve pictured how something should go — not in some artistic way, just practically, like the steps that make sense — and then someone does it in a way that seems backwards or careless, I can feel myself getting tight inside. I’ll start thinking through all the problems that are going to come from it. Like, “Well, if you put that there, then later this won’t fit,” or “If you skip that now, someone’s going to have to redo the whole thing.” So I don’t know if that’s anxiety or irritation or just not being able to leave it alone.

I wouldn’t say everything has to be exactly as I imagined it. I can adjust if someone has a better way. I really can. But if their way looks wrong to me, I have trouble just standing there and saying, “Fine, whatever.” I’ll want to explain it, and then explain it again, and then maybe I’m still thinking about it afterward.

So… yes, I get uncomfortable when things are done in a way that doesn’t make sense to me. But I don’t know if it’s because it isn’t my vision exactly, or because I’m convinced there’s going to be a problem if it’s not handled right.
When you think about stepping back and letting others handle things, what is it that you fear might happen?

What I fear is… if I step back, it doesn’t get handled. Or it gets handled halfway, and then I’m the one standing there later looking at the mess, thinking, “Well, I knew this was going to happen.”

That’s what people don’t seem to understand. Everybody keeps saying I’m doing too much — my family, people around me, even folks who don’t know the whole situation. But from where I’m standing, there’s a lot that actually needs doing. The move isn’t going to organize itself. The new garage isn’t going to build itself right if nobody is paying attention to the details. Things at church don’t just fall into place because everyone means well. And at work, those younger fellows… they’re good boys, some of them, but they don’t always know the proper way yet, and somebody has to show them before they make habits out of doing it wrong.

So when you ask what I fear, I guess I fear that if I let go, everything gets sloppy. Things get missed. People take shortcuts. Then later it costs more time, more money, more aggravation, or somebody has to redo it all. And I know people say, “Let someone else take care of it,” but I don’t see the same urgency in them. I don’t see the same drive. To me it feels like I’m the only one who’s really willing to keep pushing until all these things are actually done the way they need to be done.

Maybe that sounds like I don’t trust anybody. Maybe I don’t, not fully. But it’s hard to step back when I can already see the problems coming.
Do you often find yourself expecting special treatment or automatic deference from others?

I don’t know. “Special treatment” sounds like I’m asking people to roll out a carpet for me, and I don’t think I do that. I don’t expect people to bow down or defer to me just because I’m me.

Now, do I expect people to listen when I’ve got experience with something? Yes. I suppose I do. If I’ve been doing a kind of work for years, or I’ve been involved in something long enough to know where the trouble spots are, then I do get frustrated when someone acts like my opinion is just one opinion among many, like it doesn’t carry any more weight than somebody who just walked in. That bothers me.

But I’m not sitting there thinking, “I deserve special treatment.” It’s more like… I expect common sense. I expect respect, maybe. Especially at my age, after working hard and carrying responsibilities. I don’t think that’s unreasonable, though maybe other people might see it differently if I get too forceful.

Automatic deference? No, I don’t think automatic. I don’t need people to agree with me before I’ve even said anything. But if I’ve explained why something should be done a certain way, and I know what I’m talking about, then yes, I expect that to matter. And when it doesn’t, I can have a hard time letting it go.
Do you often feel like your opinions or ideas are more important than those of others?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, that my opinions are “more important.” That sounds arrogant, and I don’t like to think of myself like that.

What I would say is, if I’ve spent a lot of time with something, or I’ve seen how it goes wrong, then I do feel like my opinion should carry some weight. More weight than somebody who’s just guessing, I suppose. But that’s not the same as thinking I’m important and they’re not.

I can listen. If someone has a better idea and they can explain it, I’m not against that. I don’t mind being corrected if it actually makes sense. What bothers me is when people dismiss what I’m saying before they’ve really thought it through, or they act like all ideas are equal no matter who has experience and who doesn’t.

So… do I often feel my ideas are more important? Maybe sometimes, in certain situations. Especially if I feel like I know the area better, or I’m the one who will end up dealing with the consequences. But I don’t walk around thinking everyone else’s thoughts are worthless. It’s more that I have a hard time staying quiet when I’m convinced I’m seeing something they’re missing.
Do you feel like your behavior and the way you've been handling things have caused significant problems or distress in your life or relationships?

Yes… I mean, I can’t really sit here and say it hasn’t caused problems. I may not agree with everybody’s version of how it happened, but things did get out of hand.

At work, I ended up being pulled off after a safety incident. That’s hard for me to even say, because I’ve always taken pride in knowing what I’m doing and being the one people could count on. I don’t like being treated like I’m a danger or like I suddenly don’t know my job. But that’s what happened — after that incident, they didn’t want me continuing like I was. And it wasn’t just embarrassing, it shook me. I kept thinking, “They’re overreacting,” but then another part of me knew it had become a real problem if they were stepping in that way.

And at home… well, that’s been worse in some ways. My wife and my family, they stopped trusting me with decisions. Not just little things either — money, driving, the move, all of it. They started acting like they had to double-check me or take things out of my hands because they thought I was pushing too hard or making choices too fast. That caused a lot of arguments. I felt cornered, like everybody had decided I couldn’t be trusted, and I was trying to explain that I was only trying to keep things moving and get things done right.

But yes, if you’re asking plainly, it has caused distress. It’s caused problems in my marriage, with my family, and with work. I don’t like admitting that, because I still feel like some of what I was doing made sense at the time, but I can’t deny the consequences. People didn’t just get annoyed — they started taking responsibilities away from me. That’s a pretty significant thing.
Do you often feel like your accomplishments or abilities are more impressive than those of others?

I’m not sure. I mean, I know there are things I’m good at. I’ve worked hard, I’ve learned a lot over the years, and I don’t think there’s anything wrong with knowing your own strengths. If you’ve spent decades doing something, you’re going to know more than someone who hasn’t. That’s just life, not bragging.

But “more impressive than other people” — I don’t know that I think of it in those words. I don’t sit around comparing trophies or thinking I’m some exceptional person. I’ve known plenty of people who were smarter than me in certain ways, or better at certain things. Some people can do paperwork or computers or talking in meetings better than I can. I’m not blind to that.

What I do feel is that I’ve earned some respect for what I can do and what I’ve carried. And when that gets overlooked, or when people act like I don’t know anything, then yes, I can get irritated and probably start sounding like I think I’m better than them. But inside, it’s more like I’m trying to say, “Don’t treat me like I’m useless. I’ve done things. I know things.”

So… often? I don’t know. Maybe I’m proud, maybe too proud sometimes, but I wouldn’t say I’m walking around thinking my abilities are more impressive than everybody else’s. It depends what we’re talking about.
Do you feel like things would be chaotic or fall apart if you didn't maintain control over them?

I don’t know if I’d say “fall apart.” That feels a little dramatic to me. But… I do feel better when I’m the one keeping track of things, yes.

It’s not that I think everyone else is incompetent. I don’t mean it like that. It’s more that when I’m not involved, I start wondering whether something is being missed, or whether somebody is making a decision without really understanding the consequences. And then I have a hard time just sitting back and letting it happen.

I’ve always been the kind of person who wants to know what the plan is, who’s doing what, what the next step is. If I’m responsible for something, I don’t like loose ends. I don’t like people saying, “Oh, it’ll work itself out,” because in my experience things usually don’t work themselves out unless somebody is paying attention.

But chaotic? Maybe sometimes it feels that way to me, even if other people wouldn’t call it chaos. I can get very uncomfortable when things are out of my hands. I’ll start checking, asking questions, trying to steer it back into some kind of order. And I know that can come across as controlling.

So I guess the honest answer is: I don’t necessarily believe everything would collapse without me, but I do have trouble trusting that things will be handled properly if I’m not keeping a close eye on them.

It feels like I can already see how something ought to be done, start to finish, and when people start questioning every step or trying to do it some sideways way, I get… I get pretty impatient.

Lately it’s been more than just wanting things orderly. I’ll be in a great mood, joking around, feeling like I’ve got all the energy in the world, like I’m ten feet tall and can carry the whole thing myself. And then somebody — my wife, or my boy — asks one little question, something simple like why I’m doing it that way or whether it can wait, and I snap. I don’t always mean to, but it comes out like, “Either get on board with what I’m doing or get out of my way.”

Because in that moment it doesn’t feel like they’re helping. It feels like they’re slowing me down. And I know that probably sounds difficult to live with, but when I’m in it, I just feel so sure that my plan is the right one and everybody else needs to catch up.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Are your relationships with family or friends being affected by your behavior or the way you're handling things lately?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I ended up getting pulled from work after a safety incident, and at home my wife and family stopped trusting me with decisions about money, driving, or the move because things had gotten out of hand.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether his recent behavior is affecting his family or social relationships, which is most directly about functional impairment at home and with family.

patient.answer:
Yes… it has. I don’t like admitting that, because in my head I’m just trying to keep things moving and make sure nobody drops the ball, but yes, it’s affected things.

At work, it got bad enough that they pulled me off after a safety incident. I was sure I had things under control, and I didn’t see it the way they saw it at the time, but afterward everybody acted like I couldn’t be trusted to make the right call. That was humiliating. I’ve worked hard my whole life, and then suddenly people are looking at me like I’m a problem.

And at home… my wife and family have definitely changed how they deal with me. They don’t really trust me with certain decisions right now — money, driving, even parts of the move. They’ll say they’re just being careful, or that things have gotten out of hand, but it feels like they’re taking over. If I want to make a purchase or decide when we’re going somewhere or how the move should be handled, there’s this pause, this look between them, like they’ve already decided I’m not being reasonable.

So yes, my relationships are strained. My wife is tired, my family is wary around me, and I can feel that. I still think a lot of what I was trying to do needed doing, but I can’t really say it hasn’t caused trouble, because it has.

doctor.question: Do you find yourself repeating certain thoughts or behaviors over and over, even when you try to stop?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about repetitive intrusive thoughts or compulsive behaviors that continue despite trying to stop, which is not covered by the provided Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Repeating thoughts or behaviors… I’m not sure I know exactly what you mean by that.

I don’t think I have, like, a ritual or something I’m doing over and over because I can’t stop myself. I’m not counting things or checking a lock twenty times, if that’s what you’re asking. At least, not that I’ve noticed.

Now, I do get stuck on things in the sense that if something needs doing, I’ll keep coming back to it in my head, and I’ll talk about it more than other people probably want me to. My wife might say I repeat myself, because I’ll keep explaining why something has to be handled a certain way. But from my side, that feels more like trying to get the point across, not like some thought I’m trying to stop and can’t.

So… no, I don’t think so. Not in the way you’re describing, unless I’m misunderstanding the question.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Do you think your way of handling things is causing you more problems than it's solving?

target_item.name: Painful_Consequence_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: I put deposits down on garage work and equipment without talking it over with my wife, and I kept driving back and forth between the houses and rushing jobs at the plant even after people warned me I was taking chances.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient’s current way of acting is leading to negative consequences, which most directly matches excessive involvement in risky or consequence-prone behaviors.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think I have to admit that it is. I don’t like saying that, because when I’m doing it, it feels like I’m solving the problem. It feels like I’m the one moving things along while everybody else is standing around talking it to death. But then afterward there’s a bill, or an argument, or somebody upset with me, and I can see it’s made more mess than it fixed.

Like with the garage work and some equipment — I went ahead and put deposits down without really sitting down with my wife and talking it through. In my mind, I was thinking, “If I don’t move on this now, we’ll miss the chance, or the work won’t get done, or it’ll cost more later.” It felt practical to me at the time, even responsible in a way. But I didn’t stop and think how it would feel to her, finding out money had already been committed and she hadn’t been part of the decision. So instead of getting something handled, I created a whole other problem at home.

And the same thing happened with the driving back and forth between the houses. People were telling me I was doing too much, that I was taking chances, and I heard them, but I didn’t really take it in. I kept thinking, “It has to get done, and I’m the one who can do it.” Same at the plant — I was rushing jobs, pushing through, even after people warned me I was cutting it too close or taking risks. I thought I was being efficient. Looking back, I can see how it looked reckless.

So yes, if I’m being honest, my way of handling things has caused more problems than I meant it to. I still have this feeling like things won’t get done right unless I stay on top of them, but I can’t deny that I’ve caused trouble by charging ahead.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness and perfectionism
doctor.question: Do you find that your attention to details and desire for things to be done a certain way interferes with your ability to complete tasks efficiently?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about perfectionism or rigid attention to details interfering with task completion, which is not specifically covered by the provided Bipolar I symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d put it that way exactly.

I mean, I do like things done correctly. I’ve worked around machinery and jobs where if somebody skips a step or does it sloppy, it can matter. So I’ve always paid attention to how things are done, and I can get irritated if people act like “close enough” is good enough. But I don’t think I’m sitting there polishing one tiny detail so long that nothing gets finished.

If anything, lately people would probably say I’m going too fast, not too slow. My problem hasn’t felt like getting stuck on details — it’s more that I see what needs doing and I want it handled, and I don’t have much patience for waiting around or rehashing it over and over.

Now, maybe my wife would say I have a certain way I want things done and I push that too hard. I can see that. If I think a job should be done in a particular order, I’ll keep explaining it, and I may not leave much room for somebody else’s way. But in my mind that’s about being efficient, not being unable to finish.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed that attention to details is keeping me from completing tasks efficiently. If there’s interference, it’s probably more in how I deal with people when I think something needs to get done a certain way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Do you feel like your behavior or the way you've been handling things lately is significantly impacting your daily life or relationships in a negative way?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I ended up getting pulled from work after a safety incident, and at home my wife and family stopped trusting me with decisions about money, driving, or the move because things had gotten out of hand.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the recent behavior has negatively affected daily life and relationships, which is directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean… yes, it has. I wish I could say it was just people overreacting or not understanding what I was trying to do, but it’s gotten to the point where there have been real consequences.

At work, I ended up being pulled off after a safety incident. That’s not a small thing. I’ve worked around equipment for years, so being told I couldn’t keep going because of how I was handling things — that hit me hard. In my head I thought I was just moving fast and getting things done, but other people saw it as unsafe, and apparently it was serious enough that they took me out of it.

And at home it’s affected just about everything. My wife and family don’t really trust me right now with decisions — money decisions, driving back and forth, things about the move. They’ve started stepping in or questioning me because they feel like things got out of hand. I don’t like being treated like I can’t make my own choices, but I also can’t pretend they’re making it up. I did make decisions without talking them through, and I pushed ahead when people were telling me to slow down.

So yes, it’s impacted my daily life and relationships. It’s caused arguments, it’s made my family nervous around my judgment, and it’s affected my work. That’s hard for me to admit, but it’s true.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is due to a need for control or perfectionism
doctor.question: Do you feel like things would fall apart or not meet your standards if you weren't in charge of them?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because everyone says I’ve been doing too much, but to me it feels like I’m the only one with enough drive to get the move handled, rebuild the new garage right, organize things at church, and still show the younger fellows at work how the job ought to be done.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about feeling the need to be in charge so tasks get done properly, which best matches the increased goal-directed drive to manage the move, garage, church, and work because I feel like I’m the only one who can keep it all handled.

patient.answer:
Yes… I suppose I do feel that way. Maybe more than I want to admit.

It’s not like I wake up thinking, “I have to control everything.” I don’t see it that way in the moment. What I feel is that there are all these things that need doing, and if I don’t push them forward, they’re either not going to happen, or they’re going to be done halfway. The move, for example — there’s just so much involved, and I keep thinking, “Somebody has to keep this moving.” And with the new garage, I want it rebuilt right, not patched together or delayed until everyone forgets what needed to be done.

And it’s not only at home. At church, if things are disorganized, I start seeing what needs to be arranged and who should be doing what, and I feel like I can help get it straightened out. Then at work, with the younger fellows, I find myself wanting to show them how the job ought to be done, because I’ve been doing this kind of work a long time and I know when someone is cutting corners or not thinking ahead.

So yes, I’m here because everyone says I’ve been doing too much, but from inside my own head it feels more like I’m the only one with enough drive to keep all these things from slipping. I know that probably sounds arrogant, and I don’t mean it that way. It just feels like if I step back, things won’t be handled the way they should be.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a need for perfection
doctor.question: Do you feel like things have to be perfect, or as close to perfect as possible, for you to consider them done?

target_item.reason: The question is about perfectionism or needing tasks to be nearly perfect before considering them complete, which is not covered by the listed Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Perfect? No… I don’t think I’d use that word.

I mean, there are things I want done properly. If something is supposed to be level, safe, lined up, measured right — then yes, I don’t like calling it finished if it’s obviously wrong. That’s just how I was brought up and how I worked. In the kind of work I’ve done, you can’t just say, “Well, it’s mostly okay,” if mostly okay means somebody gets hurt or the machine doesn’t run right.

But “perfect” sounds like I’m standing there unable to move on because one little thing is off, and I don’t really see myself that way. I’m not saying every screw has to shine or every corner has to look brand new before I’ll accept it. I can live with things being good enough if they’re actually good enough.

What bothers me is when people say something is done and I can tell they rushed it or skipped parts, or they didn’t think through what happens next. Then I have a hard time letting it go. I’ll keep pointing it out, and maybe I push too much, because in my mind I’m thinking, “If we’re doing it, why not do it right the first time?”

So… no, not perfect exactly. But I do have a pretty firm idea of what “done right” means, and I don’t always trust other people’s version of “done.”

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a pervasive pattern of grandiosity
doctor.question: Do you often feel like you're superior to others or have a stronger sense of self-importance than those around you?

target_item.reason: The question is directly asking about grandiosity or an inflated sense of self-importance, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific grandiosity item.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d say “superior.” That word makes me uncomfortable, honestly. I don’t walk around thinking I’m better than everybody else as a person, or that I’m more important in some grand way.

But… I can see how I might come across like that. Especially when I’m convinced I know the right way something should be handled. I’ve got a lot of years behind me, I’ve done hard work, I’ve had to learn by doing, and sometimes when someone younger or less experienced is making a decision, I catch myself thinking, “No, no, that’s not right — you’re missing the obvious thing here.” And I probably don’t always say that gently.

So if you mean, do I sometimes believe my judgment is better than other people’s in certain situations? Yes, probably. I do. I don’t think that’s the same as feeling superior overall, but maybe the people around me don’t feel the difference when I’m pushing my opinion. They just hear me acting like I know best.

I guess I’d put it this way: I don’t feel like I’m above people, but I do have trouble stepping back when I think I understand something better than they do. And maybe that can look like self-importance from the outside.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a need for control or perfectionism
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or uncomfortable when things are not done exactly as you envisioned them?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about anxiety or discomfort related to perfectionism or needing things done exactly as envisioned, which is not directly covered by the listed manic symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call it anxious exactly. Uncomfortable, yes, sometimes. It depends what it is.

If I’ve pictured how something should go — not in some artistic way, just practically, like the steps that make sense — and then someone does it in a way that seems backwards or careless, I can feel myself getting tight inside. I’ll start thinking through all the problems that are going to come from it. Like, “Well, if you put that there, then later this won’t fit,” or “If you skip that now, someone’s going to have to redo the whole thing.” So I don’t know if that’s anxiety or irritation or just not being able to leave it alone.

I wouldn’t say everything has to be exactly as I imagined it. I can adjust if someone has a better way. I really can. But if their way looks wrong to me, I have trouble just standing there and saying, “Fine, whatever.” I’ll want to explain it, and then explain it again, and then maybe I’m still thinking about it afterward.

So… yes, I get uncomfortable when things are done in a way that doesn’t make sense to me. But I don’t know if it’s because it isn’t my vision exactly, or because I’m convinced there’s going to be a problem if it’s not handled right.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's need for control is driven by a fear of mistakes or negative outcomes
doctor.question: When you think about stepping back and letting others handle things, what is it that you fear might happen?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because everyone says I’ve been doing too much, but to me it feels like I’m the only one with enough drive to get the move handled, rebuild the new garage right, organize things at church, and still show the younger fellows at work how the job ought to be done.
target_item.reason: The question is about difficulty stepping back and letting others handle tasks, which most directly relates to taking on excessive goal-directed responsibilities because he feels he must manage the move, garage, church, and work himself.

patient.answer:
What I fear is… if I step back, it doesn’t get handled. Or it gets handled halfway, and then I’m the one standing there later looking at the mess, thinking, “Well, I knew this was going to happen.”

That’s what people don’t seem to understand. Everybody keeps saying I’m doing too much — my family, people around me, even folks who don’t know the whole situation. But from where I’m standing, there’s a lot that actually needs doing. The move isn’t going to organize itself. The new garage isn’t going to build itself right if nobody is paying attention to the details. Things at church don’t just fall into place because everyone means well. And at work, those younger fellows… they’re good boys, some of them, but they don’t always know the proper way yet, and somebody has to show them before they make habits out of doing it wrong.

So when you ask what I fear, I guess I fear that if I let go, everything gets sloppy. Things get missed. People take shortcuts. Then later it costs more time, more money, more aggravation, or somebody has to redo it all. And I know people say, “Let someone else take care of it,” but I don’t see the same urgency in them. I don’t see the same drive. To me it feels like I’m the only one who’s really willing to keep pushing until all these things are actually done the way they need to be done.

Maybe that sounds like I don’t trust anybody. Maybe I don’t, not fully. But it’s hard to step back when I can already see the problems coming.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a pervasive pattern of grandiosity
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself expecting special treatment or automatic deference from others?

target_item.reason: The question is about entitlement or expecting special treatment/deference, which is not covered by the listed Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know. “Special treatment” sounds like I’m asking people to roll out a carpet for me, and I don’t think I do that. I don’t expect people to bow down or defer to me just because I’m me.

Now, do I expect people to listen when I’ve got experience with something? Yes. I suppose I do. If I’ve been doing a kind of work for years, or I’ve been involved in something long enough to know where the trouble spots are, then I do get frustrated when someone acts like my opinion is just one opinion among many, like it doesn’t carry any more weight than somebody who just walked in. That bothers me.

But I’m not sitting there thinking, “I deserve special treatment.” It’s more like… I expect common sense. I expect respect, maybe. Especially at my age, after working hard and carrying responsibilities. I don’t think that’s unreasonable, though maybe other people might see it differently if I get too forceful.

Automatic deference? No, I don’t think automatic. I don’t need people to agree with me before I’ve even said anything. But if I’ve explained why something should be done a certain way, and I know what I’m talking about, then yes, I expect that to matter. And when it doesn’t, I can have a hard time letting it go.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a pervasive pattern of grandiosity
doctor.question: Do you often feel like your opinions or ideas are more important than those of others?

target_item.reason: The question asks about grandiosity or believing one’s opinions/ideas are more important than others, but the provided symptom profile does not include a grandiosity item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d put it that way, that my opinions are “more important.” That sounds arrogant, and I don’t like to think of myself like that.

What I would say is, if I’ve spent a lot of time with something, or I’ve seen how it goes wrong, then I do feel like my opinion should carry some weight. More weight than somebody who’s just guessing, I suppose. But that’s not the same as thinking I’m important and they’re not.

I can listen. If someone has a better idea and they can explain it, I’m not against that. I don’t mind being corrected if it actually makes sense. What bothers me is when people dismiss what I’m saying before they’ve really thought it through, or they act like all ideas are equal no matter who has experience and who doesn’t.

So… do I often feel my ideas are more important? Maybe sometimes, in certain situations. Especially if I feel like I know the area better, or I’m the one who will end up dealing with the consequences. But I don’t walk around thinking everyone else’s thoughts are worthless. It’s more that I have a hard time staying quiet when I’m convinced I’m seeing something they’re missing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life
doctor.question: Do you feel like your behavior and the way you've been handling things have caused significant problems or distress in your life or relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I ended up getting pulled from work after a safety incident, and at home my wife and family stopped trusting me with decisions about money, driving, or the move because things had gotten out of hand.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the behavior has caused significant problems or distress in life or relationships, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, I can’t really sit here and say it hasn’t caused problems. I may not agree with everybody’s version of how it happened, but things did get out of hand.

At work, I ended up being pulled off after a safety incident. That’s hard for me to even say, because I’ve always taken pride in knowing what I’m doing and being the one people could count on. I don’t like being treated like I’m a danger or like I suddenly don’t know my job. But that’s what happened — after that incident, they didn’t want me continuing like I was. And it wasn’t just embarrassing, it shook me. I kept thinking, “They’re overreacting,” but then another part of me knew it had become a real problem if they were stepping in that way.

And at home… well, that’s been worse in some ways. My wife and my family, they stopped trusting me with decisions. Not just little things either — money, driving, the move, all of it. They started acting like they had to double-check me or take things out of my hands because they thought I was pushing too hard or making choices too fast. That caused a lot of arguments. I felt cornered, like everybody had decided I couldn’t be trusted, and I was trying to explain that I was only trying to keep things moving and get things done right.

But yes, if you’re asking plainly, it has caused distress. It’s caused problems in my marriage, with my family, and with work. I don’t like admitting that, because I still feel like some of what I was doing made sense at the time, but I can’t deny the consequences. People didn’t just get annoyed — they started taking responsibilities away from me. That’s a pretty significant thing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a pervasive pattern of grandiosity
doctor.question: Do you often feel like your accomplishments or abilities are more impressive than those of others?

target_item.reason: The question is about grandiosity or believing one's accomplishments or abilities are superior to others, which is not directly covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean, I know there are things I’m good at. I’ve worked hard, I’ve learned a lot over the years, and I don’t think there’s anything wrong with knowing your own strengths. If you’ve spent decades doing something, you’re going to know more than someone who hasn’t. That’s just life, not bragging.

But “more impressive than other people” — I don’t know that I think of it in those words. I don’t sit around comparing trophies or thinking I’m some exceptional person. I’ve known plenty of people who were smarter than me in certain ways, or better at certain things. Some people can do paperwork or computers or talking in meetings better than I can. I’m not blind to that.

What I do feel is that I’ve earned some respect for what I can do and what I’ve carried. And when that gets overlooked, or when people act like I don’t know anything, then yes, I can get irritated and probably start sounding like I think I’m better than them. But inside, it’s more like I’m trying to say, “Don’t treat me like I’m useless. I’ve done things. I know things.”

So… often? I don’t know. Maybe I’m proud, maybe too proud sometimes, but I wouldn’t say I’m walking around thinking my abilities are more impressive than everybody else’s. It depends what we’re talking about.

inference.note: F48.8 was ruled out as the patient's symptoms and behavior are more consistent with personality disorders, and F60.8 was added as a possibility due to the patient's grandiosity and need for control

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a need for perfection or control
doctor.question: Do you feel like things would be chaotic or fall apart if you didn't maintain control over them?

target_item.reason: The question is about a need to maintain control to prevent chaos, which is not directly covered by the listed manic symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d say “fall apart.” That feels a little dramatic to me. But… I do feel better when I’m the one keeping track of things, yes.

It’s not that I think everyone else is incompetent. I don’t mean it like that. It’s more that when I’m not involved, I start wondering whether something is being missed, or whether somebody is making a decision without really understanding the consequences. And then I have a hard time just sitting back and letting it happen.

I’ve always been the kind of person who wants to know what the plan is, who’s doing what, what the next step is. If I’m responsible for something, I don’t like loose ends. I don’t like people saying, “Oh, it’ll work itself out,” because in my experience things usually don’t work themselves out unless somebody is paying attention.

But chaotic? Maybe sometimes it feels that way to me, even if other people wouldn’t call it chaos. I can get very uncomfortable when things are out of my hands. I’ll start checking, asking questions, trying to steer it back into some kind of order. And I know that can come across as controlling.

So I guess the honest answer is: I don’t necessarily believe everything would collapse without me, but I do have trouble trusting that things will be handled properly if I’m not keeping a close eye on them.
